units.translation: The verse is defective at the end. Where βέλη [missiles] is said for τόξα [bows], as Homer said παλίντονα τόξα τιταίνειν [to draw the back-bent bow] Il. 8, 266. Bows are παλίντονοι [back-bent] which, when the strings are loosened, do not immediately become εὐθύτονοι [straight], but bend in the opposite direction. Blomfield noted this.
And Scythian back-bent missiles in his hands, brandishing them in the work of war, Ares.
now having a reversed look in his prayers
The Erinyes, making him who was fortunate without justice dim in the adverse-turning wear of life.

Where, as the meter of the strophic verses (183) demands, H. L. Ahrens restored παλιρρόχθοις [with back-surging waves], derived from the verb ῥοχθεῖν [to roar], which is said of the noise that the waves of the sea make.
Holding the opposite shore of Chalcis in the back-flowing waters of Aulis.
Suppl. 296 erroneously for τάμπαλάγματα [the entanglements]. See ἐμπάλαγμα.

Pallas or Minerva is called by the poets what in common life was called Ἀθηνᾶ [Athena] (among the tragedians Ἀθάνα [Athena]), by Homer with both names joined Παλλάς Αθήνη [Pallas Athena] or Παλλάς Ἀθηναίη [Pallas Athena].
Be the savior of the city, Pallas.
The gods save the city of the goddess Pallas.
To the ship-faring shores of Pallas.
And the goddess Pallas will oversee the justice of these things.
By the will of Pallas and Loxias.
I will accept the dwelling with Pallas.
Thus from the apograph for πανλεύκων [all-white].
And I alone was made without a share of all-white robes.
to shake, to brandish, to agitate
to shake, to brandish, to agitate
They shook their hearts with pale fear.
And no longer would my heart be untouched, but it is shaken by a dark-hued wave.
And again my dear heart is shaken.
Shaken by dreams and night-wandering fears.

I restored the true writing πάλμυς πάλμυος [king, of a king] and πάλμυδος [of a king] in the Thesaurus vol. 6 p. 108, where I discussed this word at length, that it is not a proper name but a common noun meaning king. Hipponax used the genitive πάλμυδος [of a king] in verses preserved by Tzetzes in Cramer's Anecdota Oxoniensia vol. 3 p. 310, from which ten Brink in Philologus 6 p. 70 plausibly concluded that Aeschylus was named by Choeroboscus instead of Hipponax.
πάλαμυς παλάμυος [king, of a king]; for the form παλάμυδος [of a king] declined with δος in Aeschylus is erroneous. It is a proper name of a king.
As each one has obtained his lot at the gates.
The third lot leapt from the upturned helmet of good bronze.
And I obtained the lot which I wanted.
